The Real Reason Electrical Plug Prongs Have Holes

03 Nov 2026, 02:17 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily Tech Desk · Source: www.engadget.com

2 min read

Understanding the Design of Electrical Plugs

Many household electrical plugs feature small holes near the tips of their metal prongs. While various popular theories suggest these openings serve a daily function in standard wall outlets, technical reports indicate their primary role is tied to manufacturing and historical design standards.

Manufacturing and Production Benefits

According to industry documentation, the holes are primarily utilized during the production process:

  • Alignment: Workers or automated systems can pass alignment rods through the holes to hold the metal blades in position.
  • Molding: Keeping the blades steady is essential before plastic insulation is molded around the assembly.
  • Lockout Tags: The openings can serve as safety locking mechanisms during specific phases of industrial handling.

While these features assist factories ranging from standard appliance production to modern smart home devices, not every manufacturer uses the exact same assembly process.

Historical Context: Outlet Gripping

A widely shared explanation claims the holes help wall outlets grip the plug securely. According to the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA), this concept has roots in older designs:

  • Detent Mechanism: Historically, some receptacles featured a small raised bump designed to click into the prong hole to help retain the plug.
  • Standard Changes: Underwriters Laboratories (UL) later updated standards, requiring receptacles to hold plugs securely without relying on the holes. These revisions also regulated how much force is required to pull a plug out.

Because the internal detent mechanism became obsolete in modern wall outlets, most manufacturers phased out the matching raised features. However, the holes in the prongs remained, becoming largely optional.

Practical Implications for Consumers

For everyday users, the presence or absence of holes does not affect basic functionality or safety:

  • Compatibility: Solid, hole-free blades make electrical contact just as effectively in appropriate outlets.
  • Outlet Wear: If a plug slides out too easily, the issue is typically wear and tear within the wall receptacle rather than the plug prongs.
  • Do Not Modify: Consumers should never attempt to drill holes into solid prongs, as this is unnecessary and potentially unsafe.

To verify original design standards and safety guidelines, consumers can consult documentation from organizations like NEMA and Underwriters Laboratories (UL), or review appliance manufacturer manuals.
